messages.subject: Inconsistencies in files post-import to geomorph?
messages.subject_clean: Inconsistencies in files post-import to geomorph?
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I'm very new to morphometric analysis and am trying to use a combination of TPS software and geomorph. Ultimately, I want to do a CVA or between-groups PCA to determine if there are significant shape differences between multiple insect species.

In tpsDig, I digitized landmarks and semilandmarks. In tpsUtil, I removed the control lines and made a sliders file for the semilandmarks. I can use tpsRelw to do the superimposition and view relative warps, consensus, etc... I used geomorph to import the TPS file (without control lines) and imported the sliders file using as.matrix(read.csv('filename.csv', header = T)). To get this to work, I added the "before, slide, after" header and deleted the 0 from the end of the first line. The generally procrustes analysis function completes with these two things and my consensus shape looks right (although the axes are reversed). However, the actual landmark values after import are very different than what was actually in the imported TPS file and the centroid sizes are also very different than those generated by tpsRelw.

Can someone explain to me why these are different (if this is normal) or what steps I might be doing wrong? I've attached a couple files to help explain what I'm talking about. Any help is appreciated!

messages.subject: I am having difficulty understanding how to make use of the landmarks created through the function digit.curves + a question about importing outlines.
messages.subject_clean: I am having difficulty understanding how to make use of the landmarks created through the function digit.curves + a question about importing outlines.
messages.body_plain:
Hello there,

My question is about how to use the equidistant semilandmarks that are generated by Geomorph from imported X and Y coordinates of an outline. I am attaching an image with a somewhat crude representation of the landmarks that I wish to place on a specimen. The red dots represent fixed landmarks, which I successfully managed to place via the digitize2d function and used for a GP and PC analyses. The blue dots represent the semilandmarks that I want to place.

Reading the guide there are, to my knowledge, two ways to place semilandmarks on 2D images. Either manually in digitize2d and then use the defines.sliders function when conducting a gpa, or use the digit.curve function which places equidistant semilandmarks along the outline of an object based on the imported X and Y coordinates of an outline.

I prefer the latter method, because it is much less time consuming. However, is there a way to include or "attach" these Geomorph generated smilandmarks to a specimen with digitized fixed landmarks? Is there a way to save them? And how do I actually make use of them if I have more than 100 specimens and want to assign a set of these equidistant semilandmarks for each specimen? Or in other words, can I somehow attach these semilandmarks to a specimens in a TPS file which contains fixed landmarks and have Geomorph automatically treat them as sliding landmarks in the GP analysis, or use the define.sliders function to do that?

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-mmF_DE_nRac/WeU-QtbfWPI/AAAAAAAAAFY/zfD0Ex_2VD4uzJxEcySuUBeDja8SVuy4gCLcBGAs/s1600/SK_88_Semi_landmarks.jpg>
The other thing that I am interested about st the extraction of X and Y coordinates from an outline of an image in ImageJ. I used the procedure as described in the guide but when I upload the X and Y coordinates to R and use the digit.curve function this is the result I get:

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-A5YdmU9Mw-Y/WeVA32PXIuI/AAAAAAAAAFo/xFodI4rj6-g9kpcjmNCXNmkteq1ruxyXwCLcBGAs/s1600/Landmarks.png>
I am not sure what is causing it, but I managed to circumvent this issue by using the following procedure:

Image -> Type -> 8 bit.
Process -> Find Edges.
Image -> Adjust -> Threshold. Both parameters set to 255.
Process -> Binary -> Skeletonize.
Then I use the wand tool to select the outline and save the X and Y coordinates. But when I upload the coordinates to R and plot them the image becomes flipped and the outline has a broken line in some places. However, the digit.curves function works WELL:

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-jFCc155KYBg/WeVDpfM3E7I/AAAAAAAAAF0/qTr4nUXeKnkxfsiX-vxqHmeOb3DvXDl-ACLcBGAs/s1600/Landmarks_2%2B-%2BCopy.png>
To fix this issue, here some code that some good internet Samaritan introduced me to:

h = getHeight(); run( "Make Binary" ); run( "Skeletonize" ); run( "Invert LUT" ); doWand( 0, 0.5*h ); getSelectionCoordinates( x, y ); tabDelText = ""; for ( i = 0; i < x.length; i++ ) { tabDelText += "" + x[i] + "\t" + h - y[i] + "\n"; } path = getDirectory( "Choose a Directory" ); File.saveString( tabDelText, path + "myTabDelText.txt" );

The highlighted portion of the code tells ImageJ to flip the Y coordinate system, because apparently they start at a different end in R.
What is causing the broken line in the outline that I upload using the method described above? R and Geomorph clearly recognize the
non displayed coordinates in these broken lines.

Best,

Mykolas.

How would i represent this in a procrustes anova formula? I've heard that it's represented as an interaction effect, such that the main effect of digitsation error would be:

individual*camera*picture*digitsation

?

This terminology would be a problem if i wanted to see if different cameras produce different levels of digitisation error, which I do, as this would be an interaction between the term above and camera, so:

individual*camera*picture*digitisation:camera

Which really doesn't look right.

Really what im trying to get is the main effect of each of my sources of measurement error, as well as 2 way interactions between them and camera type

Can anyone help me out?

Thanks

Richie

Hi Richie,

You will forgive me for answering with a bias toward our functions, but that is the easiest way for me to approach this.

Once you have performed GPA and acquired your Procrustes residuals, call this array, “shape”, you probably want to do an analysis like this:

fit <- procD.lm(shape ~ ind/camera + camera/picture, ...)

Note that “digitization” is not needed as a variable, as it is the error term for picture.  This formula includes ind:camera and camera:picture interactions, but does not assume all levels of one are represented with all levels of the other, in case that is an issue.  (It also does not force the random effect to be represented as a fixed effect in the model.)

For evaluation, you will want to also do this:

fit <- nested.update(fit, ~ camera/picture)
fit <- nested.update(fit, ~ ind/camera)

These will calculate F values with picture and camera as random effects for which to compare fixed effects, camera and individual, respectively.  This overrides using digitization as the error for each effect, which would be incorrect in a nested ANOVA framework.

You could also trick our bilat.symmerty function if you wanted with

bilat.symmetry(A = shape, ind = ind, side = camera, rep = picture, object.sym = FALSE, …)

The ANOVA would be set up correctly but have the terms ind, side, and rep instead of your variable names.  This function is designed to deal with paired shapes, which you kind of have with the cameras.  The object.sym = FALSE is to make sure the analysis knows that there are separate landmark configurations (matching symmetry) rather than left and right halves of the same configuration.

The two approaches should give you similar results although the ANOVA tables will be constructed slightly different.  (The former considers camera to be a fixed effect with respect to digitization; the latter uses a three-way interaction and keeps camera as a random effect.)

Hope that helps!
Mike

Richie,

See the help page for bilat.symmetry. It provides instructions on what is required. Also, the geomorph manual found on Github provides additional guidance.

Regarding MorphoJ: Yes, things will be slightly different, due to some computational decisions made in MorphoJ. For instance, MorphoJ uses Full Procrustes fitting whereas virtually all other morphometyric software for which I am aware (including geomorph) use the standard Partial Procrustes fitting.  Thus, values will not be numerically identical in MorphoJ following alignment. However, there will be a perfect 1.0 correlation between geomorph and TPSRelw for example, in terms of estimated shape differences found from GPA-aligned shapes. Other procedural choices in MorphoJ can also cause some slight differences for particular analyses.

messages.body_plain:
Richie,

Let me chime in here.  I think there was a piece of what Mike stated that was missed from a statistical perspective. What Mike was saying is that from the description of your nested design and digitization, there IS no additional variation that could be explained by any possible interaction term. Think of it this way.  You digitized each picture twice. Thus, if you obtain SSCamera, and then SSPicture and then SSDig, there is no variation left to explain.  All sums-of-squares are perfectly described in this case by these components; there is nothing left. For this reason, the nested design would test SSPicture against SSDig (with SSDig serving as the EMS error), then SSCamera is tested against SSPicture, with SSPicture serving as its EMS.

Perhaps it is instructive to think of a simple univariate case to recall what is meant by a nested model in terms of the sums of squares. Think of 2 factors, A and B.  A full factorial design has SSA, SSB, and SSA:B; the last of which is the interaction term. With a nested model we have SSA and SSB nested within A: there is no interaction.  But look deeper: if one looks at the nested SS we find that the SS for the nested term (call it SSB(A)) actually equals the sum of SSB and SSA:B from the factorial design. In other words, the nested term describes all of the SS for factor B, as well as its interaction with A (code below).  This is why with the design you described there is no additional interaction. The simple example below shows mathematically how this is in fact the case.

Hope this helps,

Dean

y<-rnorm(30)

x<-gl(2,15)

x2<-gl(2,1,30)

anova(lm(y~x*x2))

anova(lm(y~x/x2))

Dean

messages.body_plain:
Sarah,

I recommend that instead of using morphol.disparity - which just uses the residuals from a procD.lm object, perhaps generated from procD.pgls - you use the procD.lm object created by procD.pgls and create a bootstrap procedure directly from it.  You can create a for loop where in every iteration, you either resample the data (by rows) with replacement and re-obtain a PGLS result (procD.pgls with iter = 1), or my preference, you resample residuals (not pgls.residuals) with replacement (again by rows), add these to fitted values (not pgls.fitted values), re-obtain a pgls result (iter = 1) and then get a morphol.disparity result for 1 iteration.  Doing one of these for every bootstrap iteration will create distributions of bootstrapped Procrustes variances from which confidence intervals can be estimated, holding the phylogenetic correction constant (not randomizing it).  (The latter approach also holds model effects, if any, constant.)

My suggestion assumes you are comfortable with using for loops (or maybe vectorization with apply-like functions) and extracting attributes from procD.lm objects.  I’ll gladly provide more detail if needed, but chose not to get too technical for this forum response.  Let me know if you want a direct email with an example.

Most of our functions use randomization of residuals rather than bootstrapping.  Regarding the bootstrapping, there are philosophically diverse methods (as my example above illustrates).  This makes it hard to include something like this in our hypothesis testing functions.  Furthermore, the random pairwise differences in Procrustes distance you can extract are similar to generating confidence intervals for the differences between variances, which is more in line with two-sample hypothesis tests.

Hope that helps in some way!

Mike

One way is to treat this as a factorial design rather than a nested one. In that case one has main effects and interaction terms, and the camera:digitization term would be the component you are interested in I believe. I post hoc test (of disparity not means) would then allow you to determine which camera displayed greater variation across digitizing runs; which would in effect be greater error.

Bear in mind though that the latter step must be done carefully so as not to conflate variation across pictures with variation across digitizing runs.

What Mike was saying is that from the description of your nested design and digitization, there IS no additional variation that could be explained by any possible interaction term. All sums-of-squares are perfectly described in this case by these components; there is nothing left. For this reason, the nested design would test SSPicture against SSDig (with SSDig serving as the EMS error), then SSCamera is tested against SSPicture, with SSPicture serving as its EMS.
>
>
>
> Perhaps it is instructive to think of a simple univariate case to recall what is meant by a nested model in terms of the sums of squares. Think of 2 factors, A and B.  A full factorial design has SSA, SSB, and SSA:B; the last of which is the interaction term. With a nested model we have SSA and SSB nested within A: there is no interaction.  But look deeper: if one looks at the nested SS we find that the SS for the nested term (call it SSB(A)) actually equals the sum of SSB and SSA:B from the factorial design. In other words, the nested term describes all of the SS for factor B, as well as its interaction with A (code below).  This is why with the design you described there is no additional interaction. >

>

>

Hey all,

So I'm working with faces and I was thinking that when i Procrustes align my data i'd want to take the symmetrical component of variation to use in future analyses because faces have object symmetry. Am i right in thinking that increases my statistical power because it cuts the shape space in half?

And if this is true, rather than using gpagen(), am i right in thinking i'd use bilat.symmetry() to align them, and giving the function the paired landmarks i could take the $sym.shape element from the aligned data and use that as the symmetrical component?

Because when i try this on my 688 observation dataset (I have 8 observations each of 86 people: 2 camera types, 2 photos of the same face from each camera type, and each photo digitised twice) I put in the information on which observations come from the same person. When it gives me the $sym.shape output its collapsed across my 86 participants. Ideally as i want to examine the 688 observations, is ok in this case to leave out the 'individual' and 'replicates' arguments? I assume you'd only want to include these anyway if you're using the bilat.symmetry function to do a procrustes anova?

Thanks,

Richie

When your semilandmarks are still a 3D array object in R (after running digit.curves), it's simple to combine the two using abind() library (install this):

new.coords <- abind(fixed, semis) # where semis is a 3D array of semilandmarks, e.g. from digit.curves; fixed is a 3D array of fixed landmarks, eg. from TPS file

new.coords <- cbind(two.d.array(fixed), two.d.array(semis))

Avi,

You can have ~ female + type in both models; you can have ~type/female in both models; you can have ~ type * female in both models.  You just have to decide - based on your point of view, preference, and personal dogma, as the researcher who knows these data - which way you want to model these alternative sources of variation for your test of treatment.

I like to think of this as a null hypothesis test for var(treatment | other model effects).  The other model effects can be dealt with in multiple ways.  You choose the way and tell us why it is important.

Cheers!
Mike
